QF.id: IV Strategies Using Interest Rate Derivatives_69

question.text: A corporate treasurer has a Rs. 200 crore floating-rate loan linked to MIBOR. The company is concerned that MIBOR will rise and increase its borrowing cost. How should the treasurer hedge this risk?

answer.text: Go long Overnight MIBOR futures to offset a rise in MIBOR-linked borrowing cost
Sell bond futures to hedge against MIBOR changes
Buy equity options as a diversification hedge
Convert the entire loan to fixed rate by terminating the floating rate agreement

explanation.text: The Logic: A long Overnight MIBOR futures position profits when short-term rates rise, offsetting the higher floating-rate interest the company pays on its MIBOR-linked loan. The derivative directly matches the underlying exposure, so a MIBOR-linked borrower hedges with MIBOR futures. The Trap: Bond futures hedge bond price risk, not MIBOR directly. Equity options are unrelated to interest-rate exposure. Converting the loan to fixed rate may not be available, may carry prepayment penalties, and is not a derivatives hedge. Note: The basis-risk principle is to match the hedge instrument to the exposure: MIBOR-linked liability → MIBOR futures; GOI bond holding → bond futures.
